title: Day 1 — The Legal EA/PA Role, Communication & Managing Up

frames.title: Day 1 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 1: The Legal EA and PA Role, Communication and Managing Up.

We'll start with the difference between EA and PA work and the legal basics every assistant needs. Then we move through communication and gatekeeping, confidentiality and boundaries, and the command hierarchy and liaison work, before finishing with managing up, client profiling and the dossier, and two frameworks for written communication.

By the end of today, you'll have a clear picture of what a Legal Executive Assistant actually does day to day, you'll know when to escalate rather than act alone, and you'll be ready to manage up with the Three C's.

frames.title: Legal EA Task Overview
frames.text:
Six areas cover most of what a Legal Executive Assistant handles day to day: calendar and scheduling, correspondence and email, document and case support, court and filing coordination, billing and client support, and confidentiality and compliance.

Each one comes with real tasks and a sample from Elias's world, like blocking two hours of prep before every deposition, or flagging a client's retainer once it drops below 25 percent. Get these right, and his court dates, deadlines and clients stay protected.

frames.title: Meet Elias Thorne — Live Q&A
frames.text:
In the live class, your trainer steps into the role of Elias Thorne for a few minutes, in character, before you open a single document about him.

Here, take a moment to think about what you'd ask him, the way you'd ask a new executive on your actual first day. How does he prefer to communicate, and how will you know if you've gotten it wrong? What's the one thing that would lose his trust fastest?

Hold on to those questions. You'll build the real dossier right after this.

frames.title: EA vs. PA Roles
frames.text: Section 1 of 8: EA versus PA Roles. We'll look at the two mindsets, how the work context differs side by side, and the decision principles behind each.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Two Mindsets
frames.text:
Before you touch any request, you need to know which hat you're wearing, because the same request gets handled two very different ways.

As an EA, you're looking after the business: your boss's time, his decisions and the firm's results. As a PA, you're looking after the person: his family, his errands, the life that keeps him able to work. Both jobs matter. The trouble starts when we answer a business problem with errand energy, or treat a family matter like a board meeting.

So first, when something lands, we ask one quiet question: am I protecting the business here, or the person? Next, before we guess, we check what's already written down about this client. If the answer is in the dossier, we use it.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Two Mindsets
frames.text: Then, if it's honestly unclear, we play it safe and treat it as business work until we can confirm. Handling something important like a small errand is the costlier mistake.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Two Mindsets
frames.text:
Once we've picked, we commit to it. Business work gets a careful, by-the-book response; personal work gets a warm, flexible one. And finally, if we got it wrong, we say so, fix it and remember the example, because that's how this instinct gets sharper.

Think of three things in Elias's world that look like personal errands but are really business work once you think about his reputation or his legal exposure.

Here's a situation to work through. A new assistant keeps one to-do list for Elias: 'Board deck edits, dry cleaning, Meridian call notes, flowers for Sarah, expense report.' By Wednesday the dry cleaning is done and the board deck isn't. What went wrong, and how would you sort that list?

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Side-by-Side Work Context
frames.text:
Both roles earn the same trust. What changes is the setting, and what it costs when we misread it.

Picture two phone calls. One comes from a firm partner about a filing, the other from Elias's wife about a school event. You'd sound different on each, and you should. The office runs on structure, policy and formality. The personal side runs on relationships and the person's own preferences. Reading which one you're in, before you respond, is what keeps you from sounding stiff with family or casual with a client.

First, we remember that each side has its own secrets. Office secrets are contracts, money and HR matters; personal secrets are family, health and lifestyle. Protecting one doesn't cover the other.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Side-by-Side Work Context
frames.text:
After that, we stay inside our own role. As an EA we filter and prioritize on the executive's behalf; as a PA we handle day-to-day things directly. And finally, when the two overlap, like a personal matter that carries real business risk, we say so out loud instead of slipping into whichever mode feels comfortable.

Try this one. Elias texts late at night, 'Book the usual table for Friday, and send the Meridian team the updated timeline.' Which half is which, and how do you handle each?

And another. A request arrives through the firm's case system, tagged with a matter number: 'Please book dinner for the Meridian team Thursday.' It looks like a personal errand. What do the channel and the audience tell you about how to treat it?

frames.title: EA vs. PA Decision Principles
frames.text:
The same kind of request can deserve two different answers. Take a request to move a meeting. On the business side, we ask whether the meeting matters to money, deadlines or legal risk, and we protect it if it does. On the personal side, we start from what the person prefers and try to make it work.

Neither answer is wrong. What goes wrong is using the wrong set of rules without noticing.

frames.title: EA vs. PA Decision Principles
frames.text:
First, before deciding anything, we name which track we're on.

Next, on the business track, the important work goes first, we narrow things down before bothering the executive, and we know which calls are ours to make and which aren't.

Then, on the personal track, the person's wishes lead. We offer options instead of saying no, and we keep private matters private.

frames.title: EA vs. PA Decision Principles
frames.text:
After that, if a decision doesn't fit either set of rules, we escalate. That's not the moment to trust our gut. Finally, every so often we look back at our own calls. It's the quickest way to notice we've slipped into one habit for everything.

Try this one: Elias wants to move a client call to attend his daughter's recital, but that client is mid-negotiation. Which rules apply, and what do you actually do?

And one for the personal track. Sarah Thorne asks you to book a restaurant that's fully booked for her anniversary. What do you offer instead of a flat no, and what do you write down afterwards?

frames.title: Typical Work Environment
frames.text:
The job looks different depending on where you land, so learn the place before you assume anything.

A big corporate office, a law firm, a remote startup or a private family home: similar tasks, very different expectations. Something as simple as which email system they use can slow down your whole first week if you guess wrong. So the smart move in any new role is to spend the first days learning how this particular place works.

frames.title: Typical Work Environment
frames.text:
First, we fit our response to the setting. When a vendor lets us down, an EA pushes back or escalates professionally, while a PA just gets the problem fixed directly.

Next, we treat clashing meetings the same way. An EA moves things by business priority; a PA checks what the person would prefer.

Finally, we watch for requests that quietly grow beyond our job. An EA points out when something crosses a contract line; a PA asks permission before going further.

Here's a situation to work through. A catering vendor sends the wrong order to a client lunch at the office, and the same vendor is booked for the Thornes' dinner party on Saturday. How does your EA side handle the lunch, and how does your PA side handle Saturday?

frames.title: Legal Basics
frames.text: Section 2 of 8: Legal Basics. Who's who in a law firm, the life of a legal matter, and the legal terms you'll hear every day.

frames.title: Who's Who in a Law Firm
frames.text:
Before you can route a single request well, you need to know who's who, inside the firm and outside it.

A law firm has a clear ladder. Partners own the firm and the client relationships. Associates are lawyers doing a lot of the day-to-day legal work. Of counsel are experienced lawyers with a looser tie to the firm. Paralegals do real legal work under a lawyer's supervision, and we, the assistants, keep everyone's time, communication and logistics running.

Then there's the outside world: clients, opposing counsel, court clerks, judges' chambers, court reporters and experts.

frames.title: Who's Who in a Law Firm
frames.text:
First, in week one, we get the org chart and learn who works on what. Next, for each of Elias's matters, we write down the team: partner, associate, paralegal and client contact. Then we learn the outside names: opposing counsel, the judge and the vendors we book. After that, before passing anything on, we ask who owns that decision. Legal judgment goes to a lawyer. Finally, we address people properly: 'Judge Rivera' in writing, 'Your Honor' in court, and opposing counsel politely, in writing, with our attorney copied.

Think about a time someone 'junior' helped you out of a jam. What did they control?

Now a situation. A voicemail says, 'This is Mark from Harlow's side, about the deposition.' Before you call back, what do you need to know about who Mark is, and who at the firm should handle it?

frames.title: The Life of a Legal Matter
frames.text:
If you know which stage a matter is in, you can see the next deadline coming before anyone asks.

Everything a law firm works on is called a matter, and most matters follow the same life. A lawsuit starts with intake and a conflict check, then an engagement letter and a retainer. Then comes investigation, then pleadings, which are the complaint and the answer. Then discovery, where both sides exchange documents and take depositions. Then motions, then settlement or trial, then judgment and maybe an appeal, and finally closing the file.

Deals, like a contract or a company sale, run a shorter path: intake, engagement, drafting and negotiating, signing, then the follow-up.

frames.title: The Life of a Legal Matter
frames.text: First, when a matter opens, we note whether it's litigation or a deal, and which stage it's in. Next, at intake, we collect every party's name and every key date. Then, during pleadings and discovery, we calendar each deadline the moment it's triggered.

frames.title: The Life of a Legal Matter
frames.text:
After that, before any hearing, trial or signing, we build the checklist early. Finally, at closing: the final bill, any trust money returned, a closing letter and the file archived.

Here's a quick one: why might a lawyer be alarmed if you said a document was 'filed' when it was only 'sent'?

And a situation to work through. Harlow Industries has just been sued. Walk the matter through each stage: what's the first thing you do, what do you calendar next, and what does closing the file involve?

frames.title: Legal Terms You'll Hear Every Day
frames.text:
One misunderstood word can send the wrong document to the wrong place, so the vocabulary is part of the job.

The plaintiff brings the case and the defendant answers it; someone without a lawyer is 'pro se'. A complaint starts a lawsuit, an answer responds, a motion asks the court to do something, and a brief argues why. An affidavit is a sworn statement signed in front of a notary, and a declaration is similar but signed under penalty of perjury, without a notary.

Discovery is the exchange of information: interrogatories are written questions, a deposition is sworn testimony outside court, and a subpoena orders someone to show up or hand over documents. A stipulation is simply something both sides agree on.

frames.title: Legal Terms You'll Hear Every Day
frames.text:
First, we keep a one-page glossary in our own words and add to it every week. Next, when we hear a term we don't know, we write it down and look it up, or ask at a good moment. Then we use each document's exact name when we save, file or send it. After that, we learn the firm's own words, like matter number and retainer. Finally, we notice which side the firm is on in each matter.

A client asks, 'What does it mean that we've been subpoenaed?' What can you say, and what do you hand to the attorney?

Then try this. Elias leaves a voice note: 'Opposing counsel served interrogatories and noticed Harlow's CFO for deposition; calendar the responses and get a court reporter.' Pause the video and translate it into a task list in plain English.

frames.title: Client Intake & Conflict Checks
frames.text:
Taking on the wrong client can force a firm off a case, so the first job with any new inquiry is the conflict check.

Before the firm agrees to represent anyone, it has to make sure that doing so won't clash with a current or former client. That's an ethics rule. Until the check clears and an engagement letter is signed, the caller is a prospective client, so we take only what we need and we don't give advice. And intake is where deadlines first surface, so a date mentioned in passing matters.

frames.title: Client Intake & Conflict Checks
frames.text: First, we use the intake form every time: all parties, related businesses, opposing counsel, a short description and any dates. Next, we search every name, including former names and parent companies. Then any match goes to the attorney. We don't decide whether it's a real conflict.

frames.title: Client Intake & Conflict Checks
frames.text:
After that, any deadline mentioned goes to the attorney the same day. Finally, once cleared, we prepare the engagement letter and open the matter only after it's signed.

What would you say to a caller who asks, 'So will you take my case?'

Here's a situation to work through. A caller wants the firm to sue 'Northgate Logistics' over a warehouse contract and mentions the contract ended 'almost six years ago.' What do you search, what do you flag, and what do you not say?

frames.title: Communication & Gatekeeping
frames.text: Section 3 of 8: Communication and Gatekeeping. Why gatekeeping is not 'no', the filtering matrix, and scripts that redirect without alienating.

frames.title: Basic Communication Principles for Legal EAs
frames.text:
In legal work, a message that can be read two ways is a risk, not just a style problem.

Think about who reads what we write: a busy attorney, a nervous client, a court clerk. The attorney wants the facts fast. The client wants to understand and feel reassured. The court wants it formal and by the book. If our wording is vague, any one of them can take it the wrong way, and in law that can cost money or a deadline.

So first, before we write a word, we decide who's reading it. Next, we write it so there's only one way to understand it. Then we set the tone for that reader: short and technical for the attorney, plain and calm for the client, formal for the court. After that, we remember that confidentiality covers conversations too, even a casual chat in the hallway. Finally, when we have to say 'not now', we use tried-and-tested phrases, so we sound professional instead of flustered.

Try reading an attorney, a client and a court version aloud, each in its own tone.

Then a situation to work through. In the lift, a colleague from another team asks, 'Did the Meridian thing settle? I heard it was big money.' The settlement is confidential. What do you say, in a way that doesn't sound rude or confirm anything?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Updating a client on a filing you just made, should the tone be A, plain language and reassuring, focused on what it means for them? B, skipped, because clients don't need filing updates? C, as brief as possible with no context? Or D, identical to what you'd send the court clerk?

Take a second.

It's A: plain language and reassuring. Reading the audience means the same event gets a different register for the client than for the court or the attorney.

frames.title: Gatekeeping Is Not 'No'
frames.text:
Good gatekeeping never slams the door. It says 'not right now, but here's what we can do.'

When someone wants the boss's time and can't have it, how we say no decides whether they walk away respected or resentful. A flat no makes people go around you. A calm, confident 'not now, here's a better option' keeps the relationship and still protects the executive's time. And remember, when you speak for him, you carry his authority, so there's no need to sound apologetic.

frames.title: Gatekeeping Is Not 'No'
frames.text: First, we never make the person feel wrong for asking, or tell them they should have planned better. That wins us nothing.

frames.title: Gatekeeping Is Not 'No'
frames.text:
After that, we always hand them something real: a specific time, a named colleague or a clear timeline. Finally, if they push back, we listen, explain the real constraint honestly and appeal to what we both want, instead of repeating the same no louder.

Here's a situation to work through. A junior partner has asked for time with Elias three times this week and is getting frustrated. Elias has said he can't meet until next week. How do you respond so the partner feels heard and still leaves with a real next step?

frames.title: The Filtering Matrix
frames.text:
Not every request deserves the same speed, and four quick questions tell us which ones do.

When requests pile up, it's tempting to answer them in the order they arrived. That's how the important one gets buried under five easy ones. Instead, we run each request through four questions, in order. Does it affect money? Does it carry legal risk? Does it need the executive himself? Is there a relationship on the line?

If any single answer is high, it's urgent. One serious reason is enough.

frames.title: The Filtering Matrix
frames.text: Then, if everything scores low, we decide whether to hand it to someone else, schedule it for later or offer another option.

frames.title: The Filtering Matrix
frames.text:
After that, we jot down how we sorted it, especially anything we parked, so our thinking can be checked later. Finally, we come back to parked items exactly when we said we would, because a forgotten item is as bad as a mishandled one.

Pause the video and sort these four: a loyal client with a small billing question, a vendor wanting a signature today, opposing counsel proposing a deposition date, and a colleague inviting Elias to speak at a lunch.

Then think about this one. A small request comes in from Elias's oldest client: 'Can he sign a birthday card for our CEO today?' It scores low on money, legal risk and authority. Why might it still go near the top of the list?

frames.title: Scripts That Redirect Without Alienating
frames.text:
Having a few ready-made ways to redirect people means we never have to improvise a clumsy no.

There are really three situations. Sometimes the request is fine, just badly timed, so we defer it. Sometimes it belongs to someone else, so we re-route it. And sometimes the honest answer is that there's simply no room, so we say that plainly and offer something else. We call that last one Drastic Contrast. Picking the right one is half the work.

First, when we defer, we acknowledge the request properly and give a real timeline, not a vague 'soon'. Then, when we re-route, we name the right person and make sure the handoff actually happens.

frames.title: Scripts That Redirect Without Alienating
frames.text:
After that, when we're being plainly honest, we tell the truth about the constraint and immediately offer a specific alternative. Finally, whichever we use, we try to get a small yes first, like confirming what they need. It makes the redirect go down easier.

Try all three on one request: a senior partner wants 30 minutes with Elias this afternoon, and his calendar is full.

Now a situation. You re-routed a client's billing question to the finance team a week ago. Today the client emails Elias directly, annoyed that nobody replied. What went wrong with your redirect, and what do you do now?

frames.title: Phone & Voicemail Etiquette
frames.text:
For a lot of clients, your voice on the phone is their first impression of the whole firm.

A good message has everything the attorney needs to act without calling us back: who called, from where, their number, which matter, what they need, how urgent it is and when to reach them. And confidentiality applies on the phone too. We don't confirm that someone is a client until we know who we're talking to.

frames.title: Phone & Voicemail Etiquette
frames.text: First, answer with the firm's name and your name. Next, take the full message, read the number back, and ask which matter and whether there's a deadline. Then transfer warmly: tell the attorney who it is and why before connecting.

frames.title: Phone & Voicemail Etiquette
frames.text:
After that, when you leave a voicemail, say your number slowly at the start and the end, keep it short and leave out anything confidential. Finally, log important calls and return them within one business day.

Here's a situation to work through. A caller says, 'I'm a reporter. Is Harlow Industries one of your clients? I just need a yes or no.' What exactly do you say, and what do you do after the call?

frames.title: Executive Presence in Action
frames.text:
Whether you're speaking as an EA or a PA, the instinct underneath is the same: protect first, sort it out second.

Imagine someone calls asking for confidential information. As an EA, we're firm, brief and procedural: we can't release that, and we'll escalate it internally. As a PA, we're warm but just as protective: that's private, but we're happy to help with logistics. Both answers keep the door closed on what matters. They sound different because they're protecting different things, the business in one case and the person in the other.

frames.title: Executive Presence in Action
frames.text:
First, when something sensitive comes in, we decide in that moment whether we're answering as an EA or a PA. Then, when someone keeps pushing, we hold the same line. The EA asks for it in writing; the PA takes a message and promises a follow-up.

Here's a situation to work through. A caller says she's from a national newspaper and asks whether Thorne and Partners is representing a well-known CEO in a fraud case. Two minutes later, Sarah Thorne's friend calls asking whether Elias and Sarah are 'going through a rough patch.' Answer the first as an EA and the second as a PA.

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. In the 'Persistent Caller' scenario, does the EA's scripted response focus on A, immediately connecting the call? B, promising a callback within the hour? C, asking for a written request to review priority? Or D, ignoring the caller entirely?

Take a second.

It's C: asking for a written request to review priority. It filters the request into a reviewable, prioritized channel, rather than granting or flatly denying access.

frames.title: Virtual Meetings & Transcription Accuracy
frames.text:
The record of a meeting can't depend on technology alone.

We've all been in a meeting where the recording failed, or everyone walked out remembering a different decision. Afterwards, the assistant is the one people ask what was actually agreed. So we treat the meeting record as our job, not the software's.

First, we test the recording before the meeting starts. Finding out it's broken halfway through is too late. Next, we always have a person taking notes as a backup, whatever tool is running. Then, during the meeting, we capture what was decided and who's doing what, and we leave out the side chatter and off-the-record comments.

frames.title: Virtual Meetings & Transcription Accuracy
frames.text:
After that, if an AI tool made a transcript, we read it and clean it up before anyone else sees it. Finally, we give the executive what he actually needs: a short briefing memo, not forty pages of transcript.

Think about this one. The partners' meeting ran long, the transcript is 40 pages, and two people remember the key decision differently. What do you send, to whom, and how do you settle what was decided?

And a situation to work through. The AI transcript of a client call spells the client's company wrong, records a side comment about opposing counsel and lists an action item nobody agreed to. What do you fix before anything is shared, and what goes to Elias?

frames.title: Confidentiality & Boundaries
frames.text: Section 4 of 8: Confidentiality and Boundaries. Professional standards, authorization protocols, and what an assistant can and can't do.

frames.title: Professional Standards & Confidentiality
frames.text:
Everything we see is protected, but business secrets and personal privacy are protected in slightly different ways.

On the business side, we're guarding things like contracts, financial numbers and ideas the firm owns, and there are real laws and HR rules behind that, so we know them ahead of time instead of waiting to be told something is sensitive. On the personal side, we're guarding a family's privacy, and what holds that together is trust more than rules, so discretion is the default.

Either way, the working assumption is simple: if we're not sure whether something is confidential, it is.

frames.title: Professional Standards & Confidentiality
frames.text:
We treat every channel as risky. A chat in the lift can do as much damage as a misdirected email. And when in doubt, we protect it. Over-protecting costs almost nothing; a leak can cost everything.

Here's one. In the lobby, a friendly paralegal from another firm says, 'Is Elias on the Meridian matter? I heard it's getting messy.' What do you say, and what do you avoid saying?

And closer to home. At a family barbecue, your cousin asks what it's like working for 'that famous lawyer' and whether he's as tough as people say. What's safe to say, and what's off limits, even among family?

frames.title: Boundaries & Authorization Protocols
frames.text:
Knowing exactly how far our authority goes is what lets us act quickly without getting into trouble.

Every assistant has limits on money, access and commitments. Some are written down; many are just assumed, and the assumed ones cause problems. When our limits are written down, we can act confidently inside them and we know exactly when to stop and ask. For example: an invoice under 500 dollars, we can approve; over that, we escalate first, every time.

So first, before we act on anything involving money, access or a commitment, we check it against our written limits, not our memory. Next, if it's within our limit, we handle it and make a note that we did.

frames.title: Boundaries & Authorization Protocols
frames.text: Then, if it's over our limit, we escalate before we act. 'It'll probably be approved' isn't approval.

frames.title: Boundaries & Authorization Protocols
frames.text:
After that, we keep business and personal systems completely separate: different calendars, storage and devices. That separation is what stops the lines from blurring. Finally, when something's unclear, we ask ourselves three things: is it within policy, is it legal, and would the executive trust us doing it? If any answer is no or unsure, we escalate.

Here's a real-life slip: you just approved a 600-dollar invoice by mistake, and your limit is 500. What do you do in the next ten minutes?

And a situation to work through. Sarah Thorne asks you to book a family flight upgrade that goes 300 dollars over the travel budget Elias set. She says, 'He won't mind.' What do you do, and how do you say it to her?

frames.title: What an Assistant Can and Can't Do (Unauthorized Practice of Law)
frames.text:
Clients will ask you for legal advice, kindly and often, and saying yes even once can put the firm at risk.

Only a licensed lawyer can give legal advice, set fees, take on a case, sign court papers or appear in court. Doing those without a license is called the unauthorized practice of law, and it's illegal. The lawyer is responsible for supervising us, so our slip becomes the firm's problem.

The line is interpretation. Telling someone what the law means for them, or what they should do, is advice.

frames.title: What an Assistant Can and Can't Do (Unauthorized Practice of Law)
frames.text:
First, what we can do: schedule, gather documents, share public facts like a court's hours, and relay the attorney's advice word for word.

Next, what we can't do: say whether someone has a case, what a document means for them or which option to choose.

Then, when asked, we use a bridge line: 'That's a great question for Elias. I'll make sure he gets it today.'

frames.title: What an Assistant Can and Can't Do (Unauthorized Practice of Law)
frames.text:
After that, we quote the attorney exactly, or have them put it in writing. Finally, when in doubt, we treat it as advice and route it.

Think about a warm way to say 'I can't answer that' without sounding like a brush-off.

Then try this. A client calls: 'The other side offered $40,000. Elias is in trial all week. Just between us, should I take it?' Pause the video and write exactly what you'd say.

frames.title: NDAs & Non-Disclosure Discipline
frames.text:
A non-disclosure agreement is a real legal promise, and we need to know what's actually in it before we rely on it.

An NDA spells out what information is protected, who has to keep quiet, for how long, and what happens if they don't. The mistake assistants make is treating the phrase 'they signed an NDA' as a magic shield. Some NDAs have expired. Some only cover certain kinds of information. And sometimes nobody actually signed one at all.

So first, before sharing anything sensitive with a vendor, contractor or temp, we check there's an NDA on file for that exact person or company. Next, if there is one, we check what it covers and whether it's still in date. Then, if we can't confirm it covers this request, we pause and verify. We don't go ahead on 'it's probably fine'.

frames.title: NDAs & Non-Disclosure Discipline
frames.text:
After that, we keep a simple list of who's signed, what it covers and when it ends, so this check takes two minutes, not an afternoon. Finally, if someone we haven't cleared asks for sensitive information, we treat that as a flag to check, not a request to fulfil.

Here's one. A new IT contractor asks for the client list to 'set up the new CRM' and says legal already has their paperwork. You can't find an NDA in the tracker. What do you do?

And another. A long-time vendor asks for the Meridian board contact list to send them 'a courtesy update.' Their NDA covers IT services only. What do you tell them, and what do you check?

frames.title: Command Hierarchy & Liaison
frames.text: Section 5 of 8: Command Hierarchy and Liaison. How the command hierarchy works across different tracks, and what it takes to serve as a liaison and point of contact.

frames.title: Command Hierarchy
frames.text:
When something looks wrong, we don't fix it quietly on our own. We follow a clear order of steps.

Picture spotting a problem before anyone else does, like a document that went out without the right review. The instinct is either to ignore it or to fix it ourselves. Both are risky.

First, we notice. We catch the issue while it's still small. Next, we assess. How big is it, how urgent is it, and who else does it touch? Then, we escalate. We take it to the right person through the proper channel, not around them. Finally, we inform. The executive should hear about it from us before he hears it from anyone else.

Try walking one through. A draft settlement letter was emailed to the client before the supervising partner reviewed it. Who do you tell, in what order, and what do you say?

And a harder one. At 4:30 p.m., you learn that a filing deadline for a Harlow matter document was missed at noon. Elias is in a meeting with the managing partner until 5:30. How do you make sure he hears it from you, and what do you say?

frames.title: Command Hierarchy Across Different Tracks
frames.text:
Who we report a problem to depends on which world it lives in: the office, the law firm or the household.

Each setting has its own ladder. In a company, it runs from the CEO down through the senior EA and the EA to the admin assistant. In a law firm, it runs from the managing partner through the senior legal assistant and the legal EA to the paralegal. At home, it runs from the head of the family through the estate manager and the PA to the household staff.

So first, before escalating anything, we work out which of the three worlds we're in. Next, in a company, we go up through the business ladder, starting with our own executive.

frames.title: Command Hierarchy Across Different Tracks
frames.text: Then, in a law firm, we follow the stricter legal ladder, because an unauthorized decision there can become a legal problem. Any decision outside our authority is a genuine risk.

frames.title: Command Hierarchy Across Different Tracks
frames.text:
After that, at home, we go through the family's own ladder, from the household staff up to the family head. Finally, if a problem sits in two worlds at once, like a household matter with legal risk, we raise it in both.

Here's a situation to work through. The Thornes' nanny tells you a man came to the door asking questions about Elias's work and took photos of the house. It's a household matter, but it might involve a case. Who do you tell, in which order, and through which chains?

frames.title: Serving as Liaison & Point of Contact
frames.text:
Gatekeeping decides who reaches the executive. Being a liaison is about connecting people who need each other.

As a liaison, we're more like a bridge: a client needs something from Elias, a vendor needs something from staff, and it all flows through us. That only works if what comes out the other end is exactly what went in, and if people know we're the one to call. When a message gets garbled in the middle, that's usually where things went wrong.

frames.title: Serving as Liaison & Point of Contact
frames.text: First, we make sure we really understand what each side needs before we pass anything on. Next, we carry the message accurately both ways, putting it in words that make sense to the person receiving it. Then, we make it clear we're the one point of contact for this matter, so nobody's guessing who to ask.

frames.title: Serving as Liaison & Point of Contact
frames.text:
After that, we keep in mind which job we're doing at each moment: filtering access, or connecting two people. Finally, after the handoff, we check back with both sides to make sure it landed as intended.

Try walking through the loop. A client's finance director needs Elias's sign-off on revised deal terms by Thursday, and the other side's paralegal needs the same document for a filing.

And a situation to work through. You passed a vendor's question to Elias on Monday, and he answered on Tuesday. On Friday, the vendor calls asking why they never heard back. What part of the liaison loop was missed, and how do you fix it?

frames.title: The Liaison Skill in Practice
frames.text:
A good liaison carries the message exactly as it was sent, in both directions, and does it quickly.

This is where it gets subtle. When we pass a request up to the executive, it's tempting to soften it or add our own spin. When we pass his answer back, it's tempting to dress up a short reply so it sounds friendlier or fuller. Both change the message. And there's a quieter risk too: a liaison who's so careful that everything slows down has failed just as much as one who lets everything straight through.

So first, we quietly work out which world the request belongs to, office, legal or household, before we route it. That's often the real job.

frames.title: The Liaison Skill in Practice
frames.text:
After that, we watch our own speed, because a slow liaison becomes a bottleneck. Finally, if we're not sure the message landed the way it was meant, we check back instead of assuming.

Here's a situation to work through. A partner sends Elias a long, polite email asking him to co-author a conference paper. Elias's reply to you is: 'Not this year. Too much on.' Write the message you'd send back to the partner, accurate but professional, without softening it into a maybe or making it sound harsher than he meant.

frames.title: Managing Up Basics
frames.text: Section 6 of 8: Managing Up Basics. Bulletproof basics, the Three C's of managing up, and why credibility is earned, not claimed.

frames.title: Bulletproof Basics
frames.text:
Three everyday basics decide whether an executive trusts us: the inbox, the travel backup plan and the full life of a meeting.

None of this is glamorous, and that's the point. An executive judges us on whether the ordinary things always go right. A cancelled flight should be an inconvenience, not a crisis. And meetings don't end when everyone leaves the room.

frames.title: Bulletproof Basics
frames.text:
First, as each email arrives, we decide straight away whether it needs action, is just for information, or should go to someone else. Next, where it makes sense, we draft the reply in the executive's own voice, so all he has to do is press send. Then, when we book travel, we line up the backup too. If the 2 p.m. flight is cancelled, the 4 p.m. is already on hold. After that, we set the meeting agenda before the meeting, which is how we go from taking notes to shaping the result. Finally, after the meeting, we follow every action item through until it's actually done, not just written down.

Pick the basic you're weakest on today. What's one real habit, not an intention, that would fix it this week?

Now a situation. It's a chaotic Tuesday: two court changes, a sick colleague and a vendor mix-up. By 6 p.m. you realize you skipped the follow-ups from this morning's partners' meeting. What habit would have stopped that from slipping, and what do you do right now?

frames.title: The Three C's of Managing Up
frames.text:
Every update we send gets judged on three things: is it clear, is it consistent, and can he rely on it?

Managing up sounds like a fancy phrase, but it mostly comes down to how we communicate with the person we support. Clarity means he never has to guess what we're telling him or what we need. Consistency means we do things the same way every time, so he knows what to expect. And credibility means that when we say something, it's true. That one matters most.

frames.title: The Three C's of Managing Up
frames.text:
First, before sending an update, we check it's clear: does it say exactly what's happening and what we need? Next, we check it's consistent: our usual approach, not something improvised because today's busy.

Then, if speed and reliability pull against each other, reliability wins. A quick answer that's wrong is worse than a slightly slower one that's right.

frames.title: The Three C's of Managing Up
frames.text:
After that, when we're under pressure and clarity starts slipping, we slow down and restate the main point before we hit send. Finally, every so often we reread our own recent messages, because these habits fade quietly when we're busy.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias asks at 8 a.m. whether the signed Harlow engagement letter came back. You think the client said they'd send it last night, but it isn't in the inbox yet. Write the reply that protects your credibility.

frames.title: Credibility Is Earned, Not Claimed
frames.text:
We can't announce that we're credible. The executive gives us credibility, one reliable week at a time.

It comes from a few things done over and over: being accurate, following through and being on time, never letting the boss be surprised by something we already knew, treating small decisions carefully, and being discreet.

frames.title: Credibility Is Earned, Not Claimed
frames.text:
First, we build it through reliability: accurate, finished and on time, every time. Next, we live by the no-surprises rule. If we know about something, he knows about it too, even if it seems minor. Then, we treat small decisions as if they might matter, because some of them quietly carry money, legal or reputation risk, and we can't always tell which ones will. After that, discretion is our default, especially around investors, legal matters, family and deals. Finally, if we ever damage that trust, we rebuild it steadily over time. One good week doesn't undo a bad one.

Think of a real moment, from any job, when a small decision turned out to carry real risk. What told you it mattered?

And one to work through. Last month you sent a partner the wrong version of a contract, and now Elias double-checks everything you send. What does rebuilding his trust look like over the next few weeks, specifically?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Does the 'No-Surprises Rule' mean A, surprises are fine as long as they're positive? B, only bad news needs to be flagged early? C, an executive should never be blindsided by something their assistant already knew? Or D, executives enjoy occasional surprises?

Take a second.

It's C. Anything the assistant already knows that could affect the executive needs to reach them proactively, good or bad.

frames.title: Client Profiling & the Dossier
frames.text: Section 7 of 8: Client Profiling and the Dossier. Building a client profile, creating a comprehensive dossier, and setting up the trackers that put it to work.

frames.title: Client Profiling
frames.text:
A client profile is something we build once, so we never have to ask the same question twice.

Think about how it feels when a new assistant asks you, for the third time, whether you like morning or afternoon meetings. It wears down trust fast. A profile is a short reference that captures who this person is, so every interaction starts from what we already know.

First, we start with the basics: their role, their organization and how far their authority reaches. Next, we note how they like to communicate. Blunt or detailed? Written or spoken? Then, we write down their meeting rules, like breaks between meetings and times that are off-limits, because those are the rules new people break most. After that, we capture travel preferences in enough detail to book without asking. Finally, we note any quirks, in plain, respectful language.

Using what you now know about Elias, what's one question you'd never need to ask him again?

And picture this. A new colleague books Elias an early-morning red-eye before a court day and schedules three back-to-back meetings after it. Which parts of his profile would have stopped both mistakes?

frames.title: Creating a Comprehensive Client Dossier
frames.text:
A dossier goes deeper than a profile. If the profile is a quick reference card, the dossier is the full handbook, in four parts: the professional picture, the personal details that actually help, his standing instructions, and his quirks.

The test is simple: could someone who has never met Elias run his account from it?

frames.title: Creating a Comprehensive Client Dossier
frames.text:
First, we start with the firm and his role, so the reader understands the professional setting. Next, we add family and personal details, but only what genuinely helps us support him. Then, we write his standing instructions as clear rules that anyone could follow without interpreting. After that, we describe his quirks in plain words, never judgment. Finally, we run that test before we call it done.

You're handing Elias's account to a substitute for two weeks. Which three entries would they be most likely to get wrong, and how would you write each one so they can't?

And picture this. A substitute books Elias a window seat in row 22 for a London flight, because the dossier said 'prefers comfortable seats.' Rewrite that entry so it can't be misread.

frames.title: Dossier Excerpt — Elias Thorne
frames.text:
Every fact in a dossier needs its reason attached, because a rule without a reason is the one that gets broken.

Look at real entries for Elias. He needs a fifteen-minute debrief after key sessions. He follows a strict Paleo diet. He sends voice notes at 5:30 in the morning and expects an agenda by 8. He only flies in aisle seats. If we just list those, a new assistant might see the fifteen minutes as optional. If we explain that he needs that time to process a court session before his next call, they won't touch it.

So first, we put each fact under the right heading: firm and role, family, standing instructions or quirks. Then, we ask what would go wrong if someone got this entry wrong. That tells us how carefully to word it.

frames.title: Dossier Excerpt — Elias Thorne
frames.text:
After that, we write for someone who's never met him, with no inside shorthand. Finally, we compare our entries with the Elias examples to make sure ours are just as specific.

Now take one raw fact: a strict Paleo diet, with no dairy, and every client dinner checked in advance. What's the reason behind it?

And one more. A dossier entry says only: 'Voice notes early.' What would a new assistant get wrong, and what should the entry say?

frames.title: Setting Up Client Trackers
frames.text:
The dossier is the reference book. Trackers are the tools we use every day to put it into practice.

A dossier tells us who Elias is. A tracker tells us what to do right now, and we update it as things happen. We start small, with just three: how he likes to travel, how he likes his emails, and how his meetings should be spaced. Starting with three we'll actually keep up beats ten we'll let go stale.

First, the travel tracker holds the details that change a booking: seat, connections and whether we rebook without asking.

frames.title: Setting Up Client Trackers
frames.text: Next, the inbox tracker records the exact format he expects, like one-line summaries with the details attached.

frames.title: Setting Up Client Trackers
frames.text:
Then, the meetings tracker holds hard rules, such as no back-to-back sessions and the breaks he needs. Finally, we update every tracker the moment we learn something new.

Here's a test. Elias's London flight is delayed three hours. His travel tracker says aisle seat near the front, no connections, and rebook without being asked. What do you do before he even notices?

And one more. Your travel tracker says Elias prefers a certain hotel in London. After his last trip, he told you the hotel is under renovation and was noisy. It's now three weeks later and you're booking his next London trip. What should have happened after the last trip?

frames.title: Why One Client, All Ten Days
frames.text:
We use the same client for all ten days on purpose, because in a real job, what you learn keeps building.

In most training, every exercise brings a brand-new person. Real life isn't like that. You work for the same executive for months, and everything you learn about him makes the next task easier. So what we learn about Elias today, his rules, his family, how he likes to communicate, will come back in the calendar work, the inbox work and the travel planning later on.

frames.title: Why One Client, All Ten Days
frames.text: First, we treat every fact about Elias as something we'll need again. Next, when a later exercise leans on something from before, we try to remember it before looking it up. That recall is part of the training. Then, if something later seems to contradict what we know about him, we raise it with the trainer instead of quietly working around it.

frames.title: Why One Client, All Ten Days
frames.text:
After that, we let the repetition help us, because seeing the same family and rules again and again is what makes them stick. Finally, by the last day, we should be able to describe his rules, family and communication style from memory.

Write your answers down now, and come back to that list on Day 5 to see what stuck.

And here's a situation to work through. On Day 3, a travel scenario says Elias prefers window seats. Your Day 1 dossier says aisle seats only. What do you do, and why does it matter to raise it?

frames.title: Written Communication Frameworks
frames.text: Section 8 of 8: Written Communication Frameworks. The ACT email framework, and BLUF, bottom line up front, in emails, updates and voice notes.

frames.title: The ACT Email Framework
frames.text:
When an executive sends a messy request, a clear reply turns it into something both of you can act on.

Elias thinks fast and talks in fragments. A 5:30 a.m. voice note might have three different tasks tangled together. If we just reply 'Got it!', we find out three days later that we misunderstood. ACT fixes that.

First, we acknowledge: we restate the request in our own words, so any misunderstanding shows up right away. Next, we clarify: we ask only what we can't work out ourselves, and we check the dossier before asking.

frames.title: The ACT Email Framework
frames.text: Then, we give a timeline: what will happen, by when and who owns it.

frames.title: The ACT Email Framework
frames.text:
After that, we keep it short, with the answer first, the way a busy executive reads. Finally, we send it quickly, right after the request arrives, not as a summary hours later.

Try drafting one. Elias's voice note says: 'Move the Meridian call, get me something on the Singapore thing, and find out why the retainer invoice hasn't gone out.' What's your ACT reply?

And one to fix. A colleague's reply to Elias's request reads: 'Got it, will look into it!' Two days later nothing has happened and Elias is annoyed. Rewrite the reply using ACT, so the owner and deadline are clear.

frames.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
frames.text:
If Elias reads only your first line, he should already know what you need and by when.

BLUF stands for Bottom Line Up Front. We put the point, whether that's the decision, the answer or the action, in the very first sentence. Everything after it is extra detail he can stop reading at any time. It feels backwards at first, because most of us were taught to explain first and ask at the end. But busy people often only read the first line.

First, before we write, we finish this sentence: 'The one thing Elias needs to know or decide is...'. That becomes our first line. Next, we label the ask, with something like 'Decision needed', 'FYI, no action', or 'Approval by 3 p.m.'.

frames.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
frames.text: Then, we add only the details he needs to act: dates, amounts, names and options, in a few short lines.

frames.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
frames.text:
After that, we move the background below a clear break or into an attachment. Finally, we finish with the exact next step and deadline, then reread just the first line the way he would.

Here's a situation to work through. An update to Elias begins: 'Hi Elias, hope your trip was good! So yesterday I spoke to the courier, then the clerk…' The question he needs to answer is in the fourth paragraph. Rewrite just the first line.

frames.title: BLUF in Practice: Emails, Updates & Voice Notes
frames.text:
Bottom line first works everywhere: emails, chat messages, status updates, voice notes and phone calls.

On a call, it sounds like 'Quick one: I need a yes or no on the retainer.' In a subject line, it's a label and the topic. A good rule of thumb: on a phone screen, the first eighty characters should tell the whole story.

First, the subject or first line carries the bottom line, with a label like Decision, FYI, Action Taken or At Risk. Next, we add one line on why it matters today, usually the deadline or the consequence.

frames.title: BLUF in Practice: Emails, Updates & Voice Notes
frames.text: Then, we give only the details needed to act, in short points.

frames.title: BLUF in Practice: Emails, Updates & Voice Notes
frames.text:
After that, we close with the next step and who owns it, and we attach the background instead of pasting it in. Finally, we check the preview: would the first line alone make sense on a phone?

Pause the video, take a real message you sent recently, and rewrite its subject and first line with the bottom line first. Then compare before and after.

And one last situation. It's 2 p.m., and a filing due at 5 p.m. is at risk because the courier is delayed; your backup is e-filing. Write the subject line and first line of the status update to Elias.

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Now it's your turn. In the Client Dossier and Gatekeeping Practice, you'll build a comprehensive client dossier and preference trackers for Elias Thorne, respond to a real ACT-framework voice note, then practice inbound gatekeeping under pressure.
